Parametric Bootstrap Tests for Mixed Models

Source: R/bootmodels.R
bootmodels.Rd

Parametric bootstrap p-values for the terms and coefficients of an lmer or glmer model. Responses are simulated from the model fitted without its fixed effects (only an intercept and the same random effects: the global null hypothesis), the full model is refitted to each, and a p-value is the proportion of simulated statistics at least as large as the observed one. Useful for GLMMs and small samples, where Wald or F tests can be poor.

Usage

bootmodels(model, nsim = 999, type = c("I", "II", "III", "1", "2", "3"), seed = NULL,
           ncore = 1, prt = TRUE)

Arguments

model

A model fitted by lmer or glmer.

nsim

Number of simulated data sets, the default is 999.

type

The type of ANOVA table (as in permmodels): Type I gives sequential F statistics, Types II and III Wald chi-square statistics.

seed

Optional random number seed, for reproducible results; the user's random number stream is left as it was.

ncore

Number of cores for refitting, the default is 1.

prt

Logical: print the tables? The default is TRUE.

Value

Invisibly, a list with permlist (the coefficients and covariance matrices of the refits), COEFFICENTS and ANOVA (the model's tables with a Boot_p_value column). Attribute "resampling" is "parametric bootstrap".

Details

The result has the same form as that of permmodels: its permlist can be given to predictmeans or contrastmeans (argument permlist) for bootstrap p-values of pairwise comparisons or contrasts (p.method "bootstrap" in the pairs table).

In a simulation study (500 data sets per case, 5% level; dev/sim-boot.R in the package sources) the bootstrap corrected the liberal Wald chi-square test of a whole-plot factor in a split plot with 6 blocks (10% to 6-7%, as Kenward-Roger) and kept the level in Poisson and binomial GLMMs, also when other terms had effects. Like the likelihood-ratio test it relies on the model: with overdispersed counts fitted as Poisson it rejected 37% of true null hypotheses, where permmodels (Freedman-Lane on the working scale) gave 7%.

Author

Dongwen Luo, Siva Ganesh and John Koolaard

Examples

  library(predictmeans)
  Oats$nitro <- factor(Oats$nitro)
  fm <- lmer(yield ~ nitro*Variety + (1|Block/Variety), data = Oats)
  # \donttest{
  bt <- bootmodels(fm, nsim = 99, seed = 1)   # use 999 or more in practice
#> 
#> Coefficients of (fixed) effects:
#>                            Estimate Std. Error t value Boot_p_value

#> nitro0.4                    34.6667     7.6829  4.5122         0.01
#> nitro0.6                    44.8333     7.6829  5.8354         0.01
#> VarietyMarvellous            6.6667     9.7150  0.6862         0.44
#> VarietyVictory              -8.5000     9.7150 -0.8749         0.34
#> nitro0.2:VarietyMarvellous   3.3333    10.8653  0.3068         0.76
#> nitro0.4:VarietyMarvellous  -4.1667    10.8653 -0.3835         0.67
#> nitro0.6:VarietyMarvellous  -4.6667    10.8653 -0.4295         0.63
#> nitro0.2:VarietyVictory     -0.3333    10.8653 -0.0307         0.97
#> nitro0.4:VarietyVictory      4.6667    10.8653  0.4295         0.72
#> nitro0.6:VarietyVictory      2.1667    10.8653  0.1994         0.85
#> 
#> ANOVA:
#>               npar     Sum Sq   Mean Sq F value Boot_p_value
#> nitro            3 20020.5000 6673.5000 37.6857         0.01
#> Variety          2   526.0575  263.0288  1.4853         0.30
#> nitro:Variety    6   321.7500   53.6250  0.3028         0.89
#> 
#> Note: Boot_p_value is from ‘99’ parametric bootstrap samples under the global null model.
#> 
  predictmeans(fm, "nitro", permlist = bt, plot = FALSE, ncore = 1)$pairs
